content: It outlines a systematic approach to reduce the detection of new leprosy cases among contacts of infected individuals. Programs can either treat all leprosy contacts without chemoprophylaxis or administer chemoprophylaxis to all contacts while treating fewer leprosy patients. The latter approach is considered more effective for many programs. The guidance includes detailed steps for implementation, such as counseling and obtaining consent, identifying and listing index cases, tracing and screening contacts, and administering prophylactic drugs. Leprosy control has historically relied on early detection and prompt treatment, particularly with multidrug therapy (MDT) introduced in the 1980s, which made leprosy a curable disease. However, while the prevalence of treated cases decreased significantly, the detection of new cases has declined at a slower rate, approximately 2% per year. Prolonged contact with untreated leprosy patients is a known risk factor for transmission. Household, neighborhood, and community contacts are at higher risk of infection. Screening and providing prophylaxis to these contacts are critical to breaking the chain of transmission. Evidence shows that SDR prophylaxis reduces the risk of leprosy by 55-60%, with higher efficacy when combined with BCG vaccination at birth. Consequently, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends SDR prophylaxis for all contacts of leprosy patients. The document emphasizes the importance of counseling individuals affected by leprosy to disclose their disease status and allow contact tracing. Counseling also motivates healthy contacts to reduce their risk of developing leprosy through chemoprophylaxis. The guidance elaborates on the components of contact screening and chemoprophylaxis, highlighting the need for maximum coverage to achieve significant impact. Introducing PEP as a simple and promising intervention can accelerate progress toward a leprosy-free future. The document also reviews the feasibility and acceptability of PEP using SDR under routine program conditions. Studies conducted in various countries, including Bangladesh, Indonesia, and Brazil, have demonstrated that SDR prophylaxis is effective, socially acceptable, and feasible with adequate planning and investment. It is generally well-accepted by patients, their contacts, and healthcare workers. Cost-effectiveness analyses further support the inclusion of SDR-PEP in leprosy control programs. The guidance provides practical instructions for implementing contact tracing and chemoprophylaxis, including eligibility criteria, obtaining consent, drug administration, monitoring, supervision, and adverse event reporting. It is intended for use by national and sub-national program managers, doctors, paramedical staff, partners, and community members. The involvement of family members, affected individuals, and community leaders is crucial for maximizing coverage and ensuring the success of these interventions. In summary, the document serves as a comprehensive resource for integrating contact tracing and chemoprophylaxis into routine leprosy control programs. It aims to reduce the risk of leprosy transmission, prevent new cases, and ultimately contribute to a leprosy-free world.
